name: Canberra Times cryptic crossword, Saturday 16 September 1967

clue.text: Power of absorbing the whole volume

blocks.note: first meaning: the ability to take something in or hold it
second meaning: the total amount a container can hold

explanation.surface: A sponge's strength lies in soaking up everything it is given.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun covers both an ability to receive or contain and the maximum amount that a vessel will hold.

blocks.note: surface reading: small consolations, as in the phrase about small mercies offered to someone sad
setter's reading: a dicky bird is nursery talk for a little bird, and birds are fed scraps of bread

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase 'crumbs of comfort' means small consolations; here the comfort is literal food for a dicky bird, a childish word for any small bird.
explanation.definitionFit: Tiny fragments of bread are what people scatter for small garden birds, and the idiom also means meagre consolation.

clue.text: Lapsed in confusion at the console

definitions.note: a phrase for things found at an organ console, standing for the plural noun

indicators.note: something in confusion is jumbled and disordered, so the letters must be rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: An organist loses concentration and falters while playing.
explanation.walkthrough: An organ console has a keyboard for the feet as well as the hands, so the definition is a description of where the answer sits rather than a synonym.
explanation.definitionFit: An organ console includes a row of foot-operated keys, which organists play alongside the manual keyboards.

clue.text: Nobody seemed a penny the worse for a Rheinish one!

definitions.text: Nobody seemed a penny the worse for a Rheinish one!

blocks.clueFragment: Nobody seemed a penny the worse
blocks.note: surface reading: everyone came through unharmed, quoting a famous comic poem
setter's reading: in The Jackdaw of Rheims the cardinal pronounces a terrible malediction on the thief, yet nobody is harmed

explanation.walkthrough: In the Ingoldsby Legends poem The Jackdaw of Rheims, the cardinal's dreadful CURSE is followed by the line 'Nobody seemed one penny the worse!'. 'Rheinish' stands for 'of Rheims'.
explanation.definitionFit: The poem describes a solemn ecclesiastical malediction that, comically, leaves everyone entirely unaffected until the jackdaw appears bedraggled.

blocks.note: surface reading: a pious Saturday and Sunday spent in church
setter's reading: a medieval Church decree banned fighting from Thursday evening to Monday morning each week

explanation.walkthrough: The Truce of God was a medieval Church rule forbidding warfare over the long weekend each week, so a 'godly weekend' is a suspension of fighting.
explanation.definitionFit: The medieval Church's Truce of God was a weekly ceasefire covering the days around Sunday, a holy halt to hostilities.

clue.text: It might be love with a loud blonde!

blocks.note: taken as written
f is forte, the musical direction for loud
fair hair is light-coloured, like a blonde's

explanation.surface: Falling for a brash, flashy blonde could be a romance.
explanation.definitionFit: A romantic or sexual relationship, often illicit, is called this, so love may take that form.

clue.text: Myosotis enjoins she should not be

definitions.text: Myosotis enjoins she should not be

blocks.note: surface reading: a botanical name issuing an instruction, like a stern command
setter's reading: Myosotis is the forget-me-not, whose name asks not to be left out of mind

explanation.walkthrough: Myosotis is the Latin name of the forget-me-not, so its very name commands that the speaker should not be left out of memory.
explanation.definitionFit: The flower's common name is a plea against being lost from memory, so what she should not be is out of mind.

blocks.note: surface reading: an undecided respondent in an opinion poll
setter's reading: someone who holds that God's existence cannot be known

explanation.walkthrough: Pollsters call the undecided 'don't knows'; the setter means a person who says nothing can be known about God.
explanation.definitionFit: The word comes from Greek for 'not knowing' and names someone who claims no certainty about the divine either way.

blocks.note: surface reading: a heavy drinker of American whiskey
setter's reading: a devoted supporter of the Bourbons, the French royal house

explanation.walkthrough: Bourbon is both a whiskey and the dynasty that ruled France, Spain and Naples; a fervent backer of that house supports the crown.
explanation.definitionFit: A supporter of monarchy, here of the Bourbon dynasty's claim to rule, is a partisan of kings.

clue.text: A blow in the price war?

definitions.text: A blow in the price war?

blocks.note: surface reading: a punch, specifically an upward punch in boxing
setter's reading: the tactic of selling more cheaply than a rival

explanation.walkthrough: In boxing this is an upward punch; in commerce it means charging less than a competitor, the standard weapon of a price war.
explanation.definitionFit: Offering goods below a rival's price is the typical attacking move when shops compete on cost, and also a boxing punch.

clue.text: "- for the Parson , Baccy for the Clerk" (Kipling)

definitions.text: "- for the Parson , Baccy for the Clerk" (Kipling)

blocks.clueFragment: "- for the Parson , Baccy for the Clerk"
blocks.note: a line with a gap, from a poem about smuggled goods handed round the village
the source: Kipling's A Smuggler's Song, which lists contraband spirits, tobacco and lace

explanation.walkthrough: This is a fill-in-the-blank quotation: the line from Kipling's A Smuggler's Song runs 'Brandy for the Parson, 'Baccy for the Clerk'. Baccy is tobacco.
explanation.definitionFit: Smugglers on the English coast ran French spirits ashore, and the poem has the vicar receiving a share of that liquor.

blocks.note: surface reading suggests Robert Walpole, the first British prime minister; the setter means the novelist Hugh Walpole
setter's reading: schoolmasters, the two rival teachers named in the title of an early Hugh Walpole novel

explanation.walkthrough: Hugh Walpole's 1911 novel Mr Perrin and Mr Traill is about two feuding schoolmasters; the answer is their two surnames.
explanation.definitionFit: The title characters of the novel are teachers at a boys' school, so they are the author's two schoolmasters.

blocks.note: surface reading: a pleasant viewpoint; the setter wants an Italian-derived word meaning 'beautiful view', a raised turret or summer house
setter's reading: a famous classical statue of Apollo in the Vatican is named after the courtyard where it stood

explanation.walkthrough: The word is Italian for 'fine view' and names a rooftop turret built for the outlook; the famous statue of Apollo takes its name from the Vatican's Belvedere courtyard.
explanation.definitionFit: A raised structure built to command a fine view is this, and the celebrated Vatican statue of Apollo bears the same name.

clue.text: "The - and the throstlecock, chief music of our May" (Drayton)

definitions.text: "The - and the throstlecock, chief music of our May" (Drayton)

blocks.clueFragment: "The - and the throstlecock, chief music of our May"
blocks.note: a line with a gap naming a songbird paired with the thrush, here called the throstlecock
the source: the Elizabethan poet Michael Drayton

explanation.walkthrough: A fill-in-the-blank quotation from Michael Drayton. The ousel, or ouzel, is an old name for the blackbird; a throstle is a thrush.
explanation.definitionFit: The old poetic word for the blackbird names a songbird that, with the thrush, fills the English spring with song.

blocks.note: surface reading: a whimsical question about rain as if it could talk
setter's reading: the word means both the light tapping of rain and glib rapid speech

explanation.walkthrough: The word is both the sound of rain on a roof and a salesman's fast talk, so the raindrops' 'speech' is their light tapping.
explanation.definitionFit: The noun names the rapid light tapping of falling rain and also a stream of quick, practised talk.

blocks.note: surface reading: a cheerful street hawker who sings his wares
setter's reading: the roguish ballad-selling pedlar in Shakespeare's The Winter's Tale

explanation.walkthrough: In The Winter's Tale, Autolycus is a thieving pedlar who sings songs such as 'When daffodils begin to peer' while selling trinkets.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's rogue in The Winter's Tale hawks ballads and ribbons and sings several songs, making him the play's musical travelling salesman.

clue.text: A hint that the gratuity's cancelled

blocks.note: a gratuity is a tip given for service; the 's stands for 'is'
an event that is cancelled is off

explanation.surface: A waiter learns there will be no extra cash this time.
explanation.definitionFit: A tip-off is a piece of confidential warning or advance information given to someone, a discreet hint.

blocks.note: first meaning: labours hard and long
second meaning: snares or traps

explanation.surface: Someone labours steadily at practice in the cricket nets.
explanation.walkthrough: The second sense survives mainly in the phrase 'in the toils of', meaning trapped.
explanation.definitionFit: As a verb it means labours; as a plural noun it is an old word for hunting snares, hence entanglement.

blocks.note: surface reading: suffering from strain, as a worried person is
setter's reading: stress as emphasis on a syllable

explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests anxiety; a syllable that is 'under stress' is emphasised in pronunciation.
explanation.definitionFit: A syllable carrying emphasis in speech is marked or pronounced with extra weight, which is what the word means.

clue.text: He demonstrates how to do well on nothing gracefully

blocks.note: to do well is to thrive or flourish
nothing is zero, shaped like the letter O

explanation.surface: A man shows how to thrive with no resources, and with good grace.
explanation.walkthrough: In a down clue 'on' puts the first piece above the second. Prospero is the magician-duke of Shakespeare's The Tempest, who forgives his enemies gracefully.
explanation.definitionFit: Shakespeare's exiled duke is a male character, so the single pronoun stands for him.

clue.text: Perhaps a trace of something lacking here?

definitions.note: describes the mark rather than naming it

indicators.note: perhaps hints the word given is only one possible arrangement of its letters

blocks.note: taken as written, as the letters to rearrange

explanation.surface: A faint mark suggests something has gone missing from this spot.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface reads like detective work on a faint clue; a caret is the proofreader's wedge-shaped mark showing where something should be inserted.
explanation.definitionFit: Proofreaders put this small inverted V in text at the exact point where a word or letter has been left out.

blocks.note: surface reading: a joke about where to dump an unwanted lawyer
setter's reading: a place whose name, put before 'lawyer', gives a kind of walking stick

explanation.walkthrough: A Penang lawyer is a walking stick made from a palm stem, named after the island in Malaysia; so the place forms a stick with 'lawyer'.
explanation.definitionFit: The Malaysian island and state gives its name to a traditional heavy cane, so it is the place that makes a lawyer a stick.

blocks.note: surface reading: lazy, serving no purpose
setter's reading: Samuel Johnson wrote a weekly essay series whose title names a lazy person, so its fans may share that name

explanation.walkthrough: Samuel Johnson published a weekly essay series titled The Idler (1758-60), so his fans are named after it, while otiose means lazy.
explanation.definitionFit: Lazy people who do nothing are loafers, and the name of Johnson's essay series supplies the joke about his followers.

blocks.note: surface reading: the canvasback, a North American diving duck
setter's reading: the thing that supports a painter's canvas from behind

explanation.walkthrough: The canvasback is a species of duck; the setter means the wooden stand that holds an artist's canvas up from behind.
explanation.definitionFit: A painter rests the canvas on this wooden frame, which props it up and backs it while work proceeds.

clue.text: What did old Stick in-the-Mud do?

definitions.text: What did old Stick in-the-Mud do?

blocks.clueFragment: What did old Stick in-the-Mud do?
blocks.note: surface reading: asks about a dull, conservative person who resists change

blocks.clueFragment: What did old Stick in-the-Mud do?
blocks.note: setter's reading: something literally stuck in mud sank or got bogged down, an old sense of the verb

explanation.walkthrough: A stick-in-the-mud is a dull person; read literally, it is something stuck fast in mud, and the verb once meant to stick in a bog as well as to sink.
explanation.definitionFit: The verb means to sink or become stuck, as a ship goes down or a horse gets bogged in mire.

clue.text: Pope from the last of 1 ac.

blocks.note: first meaning: the name of eight popes
second meaning: 1 across ends in CITY, and this adjective means belonging to a city

explanation.walkthrough: The answer to 1 across ends with the word CITY; the adjective for things of the city is the second meaning.
explanation.definitionFit: Eight popes took this name, and the same word is the adjective describing towns and cities.

blocks.note: first meaning: a rough preliminary version or sketch
second meaning: a group of people picked for a team or for service

explanation.surface: Sketching out which players the selection panel has picked.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a rough first version of a plan and also a body of people picked out for a duty or team.

blocks.note: surface reading: going out onward; it also joins the end of the answer to make a familiar compound adverb
setter's reading: the plain dictionary sense of the answer

explanation.walkthrough: 'Forth' tempts the solver toward words for onward; it is a hint, since adding it to the answer gives thenceforth.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb is a formal or old-fashioned way of saying away from a place previously mentioned.

blocks.note: surface reading: a packing crate for moving house, or a matter needing removal
setter's reading: the grammatical case in Latin expressing motion away from, separation or source

explanation.walkthrough: 'Case' means a grammatical case; this Latin case expresses separation, 'from' or 'away', and also echoes ablation, surgical removal.
explanation.definitionFit: In Latin grammar this noun case marks separation and motion away, so it is the grammar case of taking away.

clue.text: Doctor, we get so mixed up when half asleep

definitions.note: the answer is a verb, to be half asleep

indicators.note: things mixed up are jumbled out of order, so the letters are shuffled into a new arrangement

blocks.note: Dr is the standard abbreviation for doctor
taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A physician admits they muddle things when they're barely awake.
explanation.definitionFit: To doze lightly, hovering between sleeping and waking, is the meaning of this verb.

clue.text: Drops in where film stars are at rest

definitions.note: a verb phrase: puts something into place

definitions.text: where film stars are at rest
definitions.note: read as two words, IN STALLS

blocks.note: first meaning: puts or sets something into position

blocks.clueFragment: where film stars are at rest
blocks.note: second meaning, split in two: a star not on screen sits in the stalls, the cinema's ground-floor seats

explanation.surface: A celebrity calls round at the place where screen idols relax.
explanation.walkthrough: The second meaning splits the answer into two words: stars off duty sit in the stalls, the ground-floor seats of a theatre or cinema, like everyone else.
explanation.definitionFit: To set something in its place, such as fitting equipment, is to put it in; split, the word names cinema seating.
